h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to judge which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts other settings can cut off from the outcome. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current parent value: replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts, and filling an empty or harmful slot helps; and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, pushing its effect toward zero. Directions refer to the signed effect, not its size. Disconnection makes the effect lower only if the edit usually helps, and higher if it usually hurts. If the usual sign is unclear, do not use it. When finding flaws, check this sign logic first. Replace any hypothesis whose direction could reverse through a competing effect or that relies on partial redundancy. Vary edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed node 1 gets no input, so a conv on edge 4 is cut off and its usual gain vanishes.
Edge 2 starts at node 1, which is dead when edge 0 is none, so the usual conv gain disappears.
Removing edge 4 usually hurts, but when node 1 is disconnected the edge carries nothing so the loss is near zero.
Deleting edge 2 normally costs accuracy, but it is already inert when edge 0 is none.
Setting none on an already-none edge changes nothing, versus the usual loss from removing an op.
Setting none on an edge that is already none is a no-op, whereas removing a real op usually hurts.
Filling an empty edge with a strong conv gives a larger gain than swapping an existing op.
Filling an empty edge into the output with a strong conv gives a larger gain than swapping an existing op.
Filling an empty edge with a strong conv gives a larger gain than swapping an existing op.
Filling an empty direct input-to-output edge with a strong conv gains more than replacing an existing op.
